summary:
AstroVital is a web dashboard that helps astronauts on long missions spot changes in their own health and decide what to do next. It tracks heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise and radiation dose. Readings are compared with each astronaut’s personal baseline and with limits they can configure. The dashboard groups readings into the health areas named in the challenge: cardiovascular, bone and muscle, immune, behavioral health and radiation. Each area shows a status of Nominal, Watch or Alert, with a suggested action and a log of past alerts. Astronauts can also enter a daily check-in, review history and sleep charts, and load real data from a CSV file.

This answers the challenge by gathering health indicators and letting astronauts evaluate and act on their status. It matters because on missions far from Earth, communication delays mean astronauts must judge their own health. Early warnings can stop small problems becoming serious. Crew data in this prototype is simulated.
details:
What it does and how it works
AstroVital is a web dashboard that helps an astronaut on a long mission notice changes in their own health and decide what to do. The astronaut enters daily readings or loads a CSV file: heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, mood, exercise and radiation dose. Each reading is compared with the astronaut’s own baseline (their first 7 days) and with limits they can change. A rules engine marks every reading Nominal, Watch (close to a limit) or Alert (outside it). Readings are grouped into five health areas from the challenge: cardiovascular, bone and muscle, immune, behavioral health and radiation. Each area shows a status, why it matters in space, and a suggested action. The dashboard also has history charts with the limits marked, a sleep summary, an alert log and a daily check-in form.

Benefits and intended impact
On a mission far from Earth, messages take many minutes and there is no doctor on board. AstroVital gives astronauts early warnings and plain-language next steps, so small changes are noticed before they become serious. The same approach could support remote clinics and isolated workplaces on Earth.

Tools used
HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks. Charts are drawn on an HTML canvas, and settings are saved in the browser. It’s a single file with no server or database, so it keeps working without a connection once loaded. The prototype is hosted on Netlify. I used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to help generate the code and text. No hardware was used.

What is creative

  • Alerts compare each person with their own baseline, not a population average.
  • Every alert explains why it matters in space and what to do.
  • A science-team panel lets studies from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository be attached to each health area as evidence.

Factors we considered

  • Real in-flight astronaut data isn’t public, so the demo crew is simulated and clearly labelled. Real readings can be loaded from CSV.
  • Alert limits are demo defaults, editable by the user, and suggested actions are not medical advice.
  • The app must be light enough to run on limited equipment, and usable on both a laptop and a phone.
  • Status is shown with colour and text together, and the interface supports keyboard use.
  • The dashboard should be understandable at a glance, because an astronaut may be tired or stressed.
